sentences.text: This creature possessed a wingspan measuring approximately 1.5 meters.
Its skull was notably long, featuring the largest eye openings relative to its size, with the biggest known example reaching sixteen centimetres in length and a lower jaw extending 147 millimetres.
The animal had the typical build of an early pterosaur, characterized by a short neck, a lengthy tail, and shortened hand bones.
It displayed heterodonty, meaning it possessed different types of teeth, a trait rare in modern reptiles but common in ancient flying reptiles.
The front teeth of both jaws were so long that they projected past the edges of the head when the mouth was shut, interlocking with one another.
Scientists do not know if the tail ended in a diamond-shaped structure like that seen in related species.
One specimen reportedly showed signs of fur, suggesting the animal had hair and a high metabolic rate.
The smallest known individual had a wingspan of only sixty centimetres, and no juvenile fossils have been found.
The first remains were uncovered near Banz in Bavaria and described in 1830 by Carl Theodori.
The genus was formally named by Johann Andreas Wagner in 1860.
The holotype, which is the specimen the species is based on, is a lower jaw designated PSB 757.
A second species, Dorygnathus mistelgauensis, was described and named by Rupert Wild in 1971.
It is generally considered a fish-eater that used its long teeth to catch slippery prey.
Direct evidence of this diet includes gut contents containing the teleost fish Leptolepis.
Some fossils show tooth wear consistent with eating hard food items like crustaceans and mollusks.
Researcher Padian suggested the animal was capable of walking on two legs, though most pterosaur experts believe all such creatures walked on four legs.
On land, it was likely a poor climber because its claws show no special adaptations for that type of movement.
Studies indicate rapid growth as a juvenile followed by slow growth after maturity, potentially reaching a wingspan of 1.7 metres.
Fossils have been found in marine sediments deposited in the seas of the ancient European archipelago.
Baron Franz Nopcsa assigned the genus to the subfamily Rhamphorhynchinae in 1928, a classification confirmed by Peter Wellnhofer in 1978.
This animal lived during the Early Jurassic period, specifically the Toarcian age from 184.2 to 182.9 million years ago, when shallow seas covered much of Europe.

Modern cladistic analyses have not reached a consensus on the exact relationships of Dorygnathus, with David Unwin placing it in Rhamphorhynchinae while Alexander Kellner placed it in a more basal position.
